title: A Stranger PAID for My Groceries in 1975. 40 Years Later I Found Him

scenes.text: Sweetheart, on Christmas Eve of nineteen seventy-five, I was six dollars short at the grocery checkout, with two tired children and a line of impatient people behind me. I was about to put back the Christmas ham. And a gruff old farmer in overalls, who I'd never seen before, slapped a ten-dollar bill on the counter and walked out before I could even say thank you. I never knew his name. For forty years.
scenes.query: young mother at grocery checkout 1970s
scenes.caption: SIX DOLLARS SHORT

scenes.text: Tonight I'm going to tell you what I did every Christmas Eve after that, for forty years, to pay that man back. And who I met at that same grocery store on Christmas Eve of two thousand fifteen, who finally told me his name. Stay with me, honey, because what she told me made me sit down right on the floor of aisle three.
scenes.query: grocery store aisle Christmas decorations
scenes.caption: AISLE THREE

scenes.text: It was a hard winter for us, sweetheart. The plant had cut Harold to three days a week, and we had two children, eleven and seven. I'd been saving all month for Christmas dinner. I had exactly twenty-two dollars in my coin purse, and a list written on the back of an envelope, and I'd added it up three times. A small ham, potatoes, green beans, a pie, and a bag of oranges for the stockings.
scenes.query: handwritten grocery list on envelope
scenes.caption: TWENTY-TWO DOLLARS

scenes.text: But prices had gone up that week, honey. Nineteen seventy-five was a terrible year for prices. Everything was more than I'd figured. And when the girl at the register at the Buehler's on Park Avenue rang it all up, it came to twenty-eight dollars and forty cents. Six dollars and forty cents more than I had. I stood there counting my coins again, like they might have multiplied. In a minute I'll tell you what I almost put back.
scenes.query: cash register 1970s total display
scenes.caption: TWENTY-EIGHT FORTY

scenes.text: Behind me, there were six people in line, all with full carts, all in a hurry, on Christmas Eve. A man in a nice coat sighed loud. A woman said, some of us have places to be. Mark was whining because he was tired. Susan was tugging my sleeve, embarrassed. My face was burning, sweetheart. I reached for the ham, the most expensive thing on the belt. And then a big hand came down on the counter.
scenes.query: impatient people in grocery line
scenes.caption: PLACES TO BE

scenes.text: I remember every face in that line, honey. The man in the nice coat had a cart full of bottles for a party. The woman who complained had a fur collar and a turkey the size of a suitcase. And the cashier, a teenage girl with a red bow in her hair, looked at me like she wanted to help but didn't dare. Her manager was watching from the office window. I'll tell you about that girl later, because she mattered too.
scenes.query: teenage cashier with red bow 1970s
scenes.caption: SHE WANTED TO HELP

scenes.text: He was an old man, maybe seventy, in faded bib overalls and a barn coat that smelled like cows, with a feed cap pulled low. He'd been in line behind the lady who complained, with nothing but a can of coffee and a bag of peppermints. He put a ten-dollar bill on the counter, right on top of my coins, and he said to the cashier, ring her up, miss. Keep the ham on there.
scenes.query: old farmer in overalls at checkout counter
scenes.caption: KEEP THE HAM ON THERE

scenes.text: I said, oh, no, sir, I couldn't. And he looked at me from under that cap, with the kindest blue eyes, and he said, ma'am, it's Christmas. Those babies need their ham. Then he paid for his coffee and his peppermints, and he handed one peppermint to Susan and one to Mark. And he walked out the door into the snow, before I could even ask his name.
scenes.query: farmer handing peppermints to children
scenes.caption: THOSE BABIES NEED THEIR HAM

scenes.text: If you're enjoying Grandma's story, tap the like button for me, sweetheart. It helps more people find these stories. I ran out into the parking lot after him, with my bags and my children. But he was gone. Just tire tracks from an old pickup truck, already filling with snow. I stood there and cried in that parking lot. The lady who'd complained walked past me and didn't say a word.
scenes.query: empty snowy parking lot tire tracks
scenes.caption: HE WAS GONE

scenes.text: When I got home, I told Harold. And my Harold, who was the proudest man in Ohio, sat down at the kitchen table and put his face in his hands. He said, Ruthie, a stranger had to buy my children's Christmas dinner. I said, no, Harold. A stranger chose to. That's different. And we ate that ham the next day, and it was the best ham I ever tasted. Susan saved the peppermint wrapper in her jewelry box for years.
scenes.query: family Christmas dinner 1970s ham
scenes.caption: A STRANGER CHOSE TO

scenes.text: I couldn't pay him back, honey. I didn't know who he was. So the next Christmas Eve, nineteen seventy-six, I went back to that same Buehler's, with ten dollars I'd saved in a jar all year. And I stood near the registers, pretending to look at magazines, until I saw a young mother who looked worried at the checkout. And when she came up short, I put the ten dollars on the counter.
scenes.query: woman putting money on grocery counter for stranger
scenes.caption: TEN DOLLARS IN A JAR

scenes.text: And I said exactly what he'd said. It's Christmas. Those babies need their ham. And I walked out before she could ask my name. Then I sat in my car and cried, because now I understood why he'd left so fast. If you stay, they have to thank you. And you don't want to be thanked. You just want them to have their ham.
scenes.query: woman crying in car in parking lot
scenes.caption: WHY HE LEFT SO FAST

scenes.text: I did it every Christmas Eve after that, sweetheart. Every single one. Ten dollars, then twenty, then fifty, when Harold got his job back and things got better. Sometimes groceries. Once, a whole Christmas dinner for an old man buying a can of soup. Harold started coming with me. Then our children, when they were grown. We called it Buehler's Eve. And we never once told anybody.
scenes.query: family together at grocery store Christmas Eve
scenes.caption: BUEHLER'S EVE

scenes.text: Some years were hard, sweetheart. In nineteen eighty-two, Harold was laid off again, and I had nothing to give. So I went anyway, and I helped an old lady carry her bags to the bus stop in the snow, and I told her Merry Christmas. That counted, I decided. It doesn't have to be money. It just has to be the moment when somebody's standing there with their face burning, and you step in.
scenes.query: woman helping elderly lady carry bags in snow
scenes.caption: NOT ALWAYS MONEY

scenes.text: And remember the teenage cashier with the red bow? In nineteen eighty-nine, she was the store manager. And one Christmas Eve, she saw me at the registers with my envelope, and she came over, and she said, you're the lady from seventy-five, aren't you? I nodded. She said, I've watched you every year. And every Christmas Eve since, she quietly knocked ten percent off the bill for anybody who came up short. Stay with me, honey, it gets better.
scenes.query: store manager woman smiling at register
scenes.caption: SHE WATCHED EVERY YEAR

scenes.text: So far, the twenty-two dollars, the farmer, the peppermints, and forty years of Buehler's Eve. And every single year, I looked for him, honey. Every Christmas Eve, I looked at every old man in overalls in that store. I asked the managers. I asked the farmers at church. Nobody knew him. And by the nineteen nineties, I figured he must have passed. He'd been seventy in nineteen seventy-five.
scenes.query: elderly woman looking around grocery store
scenes.caption: I LOOKED FOR HIM

scenes.text: Harold passed in two thousand eight. And I kept going, by myself, every Christmas Eve. Then with my grandchildren. And on Christmas Eve, two thousand fifteen, I was seventy-one, standing near the registers at that same store, which had become a Kroger by then, with a fifty-dollar bill in my coat pocket, watching the lines. Forty years, honey. The fortieth Buehler's Eve.
scenes.query: elderly woman waiting near grocery registers
scenes.caption: THE FORTIETH YEAR

scenes.text: There was a young mother at the register with a baby on her hip, putting things back. And I walked up and put my fifty on the counter, and said, it's Christmas. Those babies need their ham. And I started to walk out. And the cashier, a young woman about twenty-five with a long braid, said, wait. Ma'am, wait. And she came around the register and grabbed my arm.
scenes.query: young cashier grabbing woman's arm at register
scenes.caption: MA'AM, WAIT

scenes.text: She said, what did you just say? I said it again. Those babies need their ham. And that girl went white, honey. She said, that's what my great-grandpa used to say. Every Christmas Eve. Grandpa Earl Hoffman. He had a dairy farm out on Route Ninety-Six. He used to pay for people's groceries at the old Buehler's. My grandma told me the story a hundred times.
scenes.query: young woman shocked with hand over mouth
scenes.caption: GRANDPA EARL HOFFMAN

scenes.text: I sat down, sweetheart. Right there on the floor of aisle three, by the canned beans, at seventy-one. Earl Hoffman. Forty years, and I finally knew his name. The cashier sat down next to me, and the store manager came running, and the young mother with the baby stood there with her mouth open. And the cashier, her name was Katie, told me all about him.
scenes.query: elderly woman sitting on grocery store floor
scenes.caption: FORTY YEARS

scenes.text: Earl Hoffman had lost his wife and his little daughter in a house fire on Christmas Eve, nineteen fifty-two, honey. They'd been out of money, and he'd gone into town to sell a calf, so they could have a Christmas ham. He came home to the fire. And every Christmas Eve for the rest of his life, he went to the grocery store and paid for somebody's ham. He said it was the ham he never got to bring home.
scenes.query: old farmhouse in winter memorial
scenes.caption: THE HAM HE NEVER BROUGHT

scenes.text: He passed in nineteen eighty-four, at seventy-nine. Katie said her grandma, Earl's second daughter, kept the tradition for a few years, but then she got sick, and it stopped. Katie said, Grandma always wondered if anybody remembered him. If it had ever mattered to anybody. I took Katie's hands, and I said, honey, I've done it every year for forty years. In his words. It mattered.
scenes.query: two women holding hands in grocery store
scenes.caption: IT MATTERED

scenes.text: Katie said, my grandma kept his feed cap. It's still hanging on a nail in her kitchen. And she said, his truck was a green nineteen fifty-nine Ford, and he always carried a bag of peppermints in the glove box, for children. I started crying all over again, because I remembered that peppermint in Susan's little hand. Forty years, and the peppermints were still the same.
scenes.query: old green pickup truck in snow
scenes.caption: PEPPERMINTS IN THE GLOVE BOX

scenes.text: Katie took me to see her grandmother, Earl's daughter, Mary, the day after Christmas, at a nursing home in Shelby. She was ninety. And when I told her the story, the ham, the peppermints, forty years of Buehler's Eve, she held my hand and cried and said, Daddy would be so happy. He always said one ham was a drop in the bucket. Now I know it was a whole river.
scenes.query: elderly woman in nursing home holding hands
scenes.caption: A WHOLE RIVER

scenes.text: Every Christmas Eve now, Katie and I do it together, sweetheart. And her children. And mine. And my grandchildren. Last year, there were fourteen of us, spread out across three grocery stores in Mansfield, with envelopes of money. And every one of us says the same words. It's Christmas. Those babies need their ham. And every one of us leaves before they can say thank you.
scenes.query: family members with envelopes in grocery store
scenes.caption: FOURTEEN OF US

scenes.text: Here's what I want you to remember, honey. You can't always pay back the person who helped you. But you can always pay it forward. And sometimes, if you're lucky, it finds its way back home. Tell me in the comments, sweetheart, has a stranger ever paid for something for you? There are more of my family's stories in the playlist right there on your screen. Good night. Merry Christmas.
scenes.query: Christmas ham on family table candlelight
scenes.caption: PAY IT FORWARD
